Gun Licencing - Left Defenceless

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
If the Firearms Control Amendment Bill is passed, citizens of South Africa will no longer be able to possess or apply for a gun licence on the basis of self defense.

Unique Selling Point:
After it was published in the Government Gazette social media was ablaze with outraged citizens, gun owners associations, civil society and political parties comments on the Bill. In the main, the proposed amendments have been met with harsh criticism, with many questioning why government wants to disarm civilians, when violent crime remains an everyday reality for many people. Meanwhile, the past week has also seen numerous reports on the chaos that exists at the Central Firearms Registry, after a parliamentary oversight committee visited their offices and pictures and videos of firearm license applications literally filling the hallways, tables and chairs of the CFR's offices surfaced. The backlog runs into the tens of thousands.

Summary:
Since the gazetting of the bill, Police Minister Bheki Cele has said that they did not take the decision lightly, and that in fact the bill would help to protect many women who lived in fear of gender based violence. He has repeatedly stated that significant research into the subject has been done, and also that all stakeholders had been consulted. But many groups like Gun Owners SA say they were not consulted, and have in fact been asking for consultations with police for many years. Either way, the minister has not provided any studies/documentation/research to back up his claims that the new bill will make South Africa a safer place.

Further information:
We have arranged for filming on a gun range, for interviews and links

We have asked the Minister, as well as the Civilian Secratariat for Police, the organisation which guides the minister on policy decisions, for an interview.

We have confiration on interviews with many key roleplayers in the sector.

We have a lot of social media footage we could use in terms of the everyday violence South Africans live with.

I am trying to find a case study for and against the amendment- someone who has been saved from a violent situation because they had their firearm with them etc

Mr. Martin Hood Attorney
Mr. Paul Oxley Gun Owners SA
Miss. Tshepi Mekwa Girls on Fire

Press Release:


Up in Arms

Do you own a firearm to defend yourself? The publication of the Draft Firearms Control Amendment Bill has been met with a social media firestorm and swift public outcry aimed at the Minister of Police, Bheki Cele. One of the most contentious proposals it contains, is that firearm owners will no longer be able to apply for a gun licence on the basis of self-defence. The bill makes it clear that government wants to reduce the number of firearms in circulation as part of its efforts to curb violent crime. Would it help, for instance, to protect women who live in fear of gender-based violence if the proposal succeeds? The government maintains the proposal is based on solid research and emotions run high on both sides. Carte Blanche investigates the hotly contested topic.

Producer: Graham Coetzer | Presenter: Bongani Bingwa

Watch the trailer

Script:


Left Defenceless
First Draft Script
02 June 2021


Voice
On the 21st of May the draft Firearms Control Amendment Bill was published in the Government Gazette and opened to public comment. A highly contentious amendment in the document seeks to repeal section 13 of the existing act - meaning civilians will no longer be able to apply for a gun licence on the basis of self defence.

The bill was put forward by the Civilian Secretariat for police, the body that advises Minister Bheki Cele on policy and strategy. Within a matter of days they’d received more than 17000 written submissions - with many private gun owners, pro-firearm organisations and political parties fiercely opposed to the bill.

Link Bongani
They argue that in a country that is overrun by crime, and where criminals often show up with one of these, is it a good idea to disarm law abiding citizens?

Voice
One man who’s been vocal in his criticism is Paul Oxley, Chairperson of Gun Owners of South Africa.

Sound Up Paul Oxley
The police are absolutely silent on how to remove firearms from criminal hands, in fact in the same week that the police minister announced this bill…he announced that he was taking R3 billion from the police’s ordinary policing budget, adding to the VIP protection budget, and leaves South African citizens out in the cold.

Voice
Scenes like these - of violent crimes perpetrated by armed criminals - are an everyday occurrence on the streets of South Africa. And the police contend that many of those firearms have made it into the illicit market after being stolen from licensed gun owners.

Sound Up Paul Oxley
Bongani: But Paul, guns don’t necessarily make us safer?

Paul: Bad people with guns don’t make us safer, in the last couple of days we’ve had reports come in of people defending themselves against armed attackers with firearms. None the less, when that happens, that’s a crime against the law abiding citizen, it’s not the law abiding citizen being a problem.

Voice
We asked both the Minister and Secretary of Police for interviews, but they referred us to Advocate Lungelwa Shandu instead. She is the chairperson of the Firearms Appeal Board.

Sound Up Advocate Lungelwa Shandu
Bongani: Why does the draft amendment bill seek to remove self defence as a valid reason for firearm ownership?

Lungelwa: Licenses issued for self defence, they account for the majority of firearms that are lost in private hands. And these firearms, are the firearms that in the main, end up as being used in the commission of crime.

Bongani: But we also know that there are many crimes that are committed using firearms that have been lost say for example from the military, from the police. We also know that there are firearms that come into this country illegally, surely you cannot blame all violent crime on guns lost by private owners?

Lungelwa: True, we cannot blame all violent crime, but we can blame the majority of the violent crime.

Voice
Attorney Martin Hood specialises in firearm law, and represents many pro-gun stakeholders.

Sound Up Martin Hood
These proposals are completely and utterly unjustified. We have fundamental problems with the implementation and administration of the current legislation… To come along with new proposals that are going to make the administration more complicated is simply not feasible, that’s without even talking about the substance of the proposals.

Voice
Last month, MP’s were left unimpressed when a visit by the Portfolio Committee on Police revealed the chaos and massive backlogs at the Central Firearms Registry - with unprocessed license applications literally littering the offices and hallways.

Hood also has concerns about proposals in the bill to put tougher restrictions on the Private Security Industry’s access to firearms.

Sound Up Martin
We’ve got armed response, we’ve got cash in transit, we’ve got estate security, we’ve got shopping centre security. That’s all supported by armed reaction officers. And the private security industry, which I represent, so I can speak to this as a fact, the private security industry is a growth industry and it’s directly related to the deteriorating ability of the police to actually police.

Sound Up Advocate Shandu
Bongani: Do those amendments mean that you are going to limit the number of firearms that security companies may possess?

Lungelwa: No, the amendments mean that a security company must motivate. Give an explanation. And the registrar, based on the information that you have submitted, will then exercise a discretion, and then decide based on the facts whether you do deserve the number of firearms you’ve applied for.

Link Bongani
While some of the amendments have the pro-gun lobby fuming, there are clauses in the document that have been welcomed by the anti-gun groups.

Voice
Adele Kirsten is the director of NGO Gun Free South Africa - and says the proposed bill is a step in the right direction.

Sound Up Adele
Bongani: The draft Firearms Amendment Bill has caused quite a stir - you welcome it?

Adele: We definitely welcome it, and we welcome it for a number of reasons. IF one looks at the entire bill, one sees really strong intervention to limit weapons. Now that’s a universal principal that’s applied in all gun laws across the world.

Bongani: The nub of the objection for many people is the issue of self defence. Why is that not a good enough reason to own a gun?

Adele: There are a number of reasons for that, certainly in the South African context with our high levels of violent crime…the latest SAPS data shows that something between 20 to 24 guns a day are lost and stolen from civilians.

Voice
According to the police’s 2019 annual report, 8007 civilian firearms were lost or stolen during the reporting period. The data also shows that only 673 police owned guns were lost or stolen at the same time. But Paul Oxley says the police are just as much to blame.

Sound Up Paul Oxley
Colonel Chris Prinsloo, when he was the most senior official in South Gauteng in the South African police service, stole more than 2500 firearms to sell to the Cape Flats gangs.

Voice
In 2016, Prinsloo was sentenced to 18 years behind bars for his role in the theft of about R9 million worth of firearms from a South African Police Service armoury.

Sound Up Paul
More than a thousand murders have been linked to those firearms, including the murders of more than 200 children.

Voice
Countries such as Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom explicitly prohibit owning a firearm for self defence. Organisations like Gun Free South Africa hope that the amendments could also help in the fight against gender based violence.

Sound Up Adele
The issue for many women is about the gun in the hands of an abusive male partner.

Voice
But Thsepi Mmekwa from Girls on Fire, who introduces and trains women in responsible firearm use, says for a woman, owning a gun could make all the difference.

Sound Up Thsepi
Tshepi: Woman are in trouble, and getting slaughtered in the streets of South Africa. With a firearm, it levels the playing field.

Bongani: You run this program where you train women, in terms of how to use a firearm. What does it do for the women who are part of your program?

Tshepi: A lot of confidence, Bongani you see a lot of mindset changes for these women. You see them taking control back, for themselves, they feel empowered.

Voice
Advocate Shandu says there are currently only 1.6 million licensed civilian firearm owners in the country - meaning the vast majority of our population does not own a gun for self defence. And she’s convinced the benefits of the the proposed bill outweigh the risks.

Sound Up Adv Shandu
Between 2009 and 2014, private citizens lost over 200 000 firearms. So the question then that must be asked, is where are those firearms? They couldn’t just of disappeared, those firearms are in the hands of criminals in the majority of instances. And then these are the firearms that end up being used, to terrorise the whole nation.



Voice
But for many gun owners, that argument simply doesn’t hold water.

Sound Up Paul Oxley
Legally owned cars have been hijacked from people and been used in cash in transit robberies. Do we conquer cash in transit robberies by taking cars away from people? No we don’t even propose that. There’s no other aspect of the law, of criminality, where they propose to make the victims, to blame the victims for the crimes. Except with firearms. When it comes to firearms, it seems that it’s open season on gun owners.

Voice
Should the bill eventually pass in it’s current form, firearm owners who have licenses for self defence will have to get rid of their guns by the time their existing licenses expire. And you’ll only be able to apply for a license under sports shooting, hunting or as a security officer or company. For now, members of the public who wish to have their voices heard have until the 5th of July to do so.

Sound Up Martin hood
But ultimately, ultimately, we need to have a more serious debate than you lose your guns so don’t come and point fingers at me. Again to use a cliche’, you can take my firearms away, the criminal next door, he’s not going to hand in his firearms, he’s going to come and take advantage of me with his firearms.




Promo 1
The police believe most of the firearms used in violent crimes have ended up in criminal hands after being stolen from law abiding citizens - a closer look at a hotly contested debate.

Promo 2
Will removing firearms from the general public really solve South Africa’s violent crime epidemic? The police minister certainly seems to think so, but many others don’t.

Promo 3
If a draft bill is passed in parliament, you’ll no longer be able to claim self defence as a valid reason to own a firearm - a solution to gun violence or will the public become sitting ducks?
